title: OOM surge during autoscaler failover - post-incident notes
body:
Summary:

On 2024-10-11 between 03:12–03:48 UTC we had a multi-cluster incident where multiple serving pods experienced OOM kills in a ~10 minute window during an autoscaler failover triggered by a partial region maintenance event. The immediate customer impact was increased tail latency and ~3% request error rate for ~35 minutes across hosted inference endpoints using our default medium GPU pool. No data loss, but several high-throughput customers saw elevated retry rates and transient errors.

Impact: 
- Duration: ~36 minutes of elevated errors; full traffic normalization ~60 minutes due to gradual cluster rebalance and cache warmups.
- Affected: medium-gpu pool (us-west-2 primary), ~120 pods cycled; ~18 pods OOM-killed and restarted repeatedly.
- Symptoms: sudden spike in per-pod memory usage, KV cache growth beyond configured soft limit, prefetch jobs multiplying, continuous-batching queue length spiked causing long-lived KV handle retention.

How we detected it:
- Pager alerts: memory OOM spike alert fired for pool 'medium-gpu-usw2' at 03:14 UTC.
- Observability: per-pod memory graphs in Console showed memory increase starting ~03:09 UTC, sharp climbs 03:12–03:18 UTC.
- SRE on-call saw concurrent autoscaler ScaleDown/ScaleUp churn in audit logs and a maintenance announcement from cloud provider.

Initial hypothesis (during on-call):
- Autoscaler failover (removal + rapid replacement of nodes) caused many pods to reschedule simultaneously onto fewer nodes.
- Prefetch logic aggressively repopulated KV cache after pod restart and continuous-batching inflight requests caused KV cache to retain stale references -> memory pressure.
- Background prefetch tasks executed with backoff misconfigured (no jitter) and retried aggressively on miss, causing amplification.

Timeline (high level):
- 03:05 UTC: Cloud provider maintenance triggers partial host evacuation event in us-west-2.
- 03:09 UTC: Serving nodes show increased pod eviction events (graceful) and cluster autoscaler starts replacing capacity.
- 03:12 UTC: First OOM observed on pod redwood-srv-007 (OOMKill). Memory rose from 45GB -> 98GB in ~90s.
- 03:14 UTC: Pager fired; SRE triage.
- 03:16 UTC: Observability team identifies surge in KV cache resident size and prefetch rate across restarted pods.
- 03:22 UTC: Temporary mitigation applied: scale up medium-gpu pool by +30% (manual override) and disable aggressive prefetch via feature-flag.
- 03:34 UTC: Prefetch disabled; memory growth stabilizes; OOMs stop.
- 03:48 UTC: Autoscaler revert and gradual traffic rebalance completes; remaining warmup takes until ~04:30 UTC.

Root cause analysis (what we believe happened):
1) Scheduling churn caused many pods to restart concurrently onto limited capacity leading to hotspots.
2) On restart, our serving runtime aggressively kicks off prefetch tasks to rebuild KV caches based on async prefetch config. Prefetch tasks were not rate-limited across pod restarts and had no cluster-wide damping.
3) Continuous-batching subsystem retained references to prefetch inflight batches and did not release them promptly on context cancellation during reschedule flapping; residual KV handles accumulated.
4) The autoscaler reacted to transient capacity signals and attempted to replace capacity but the timing created a momentary undersupply where memory pressure became critical.
5) There is also evidence of a GC/allocator fragmentation effect in our modified runtime that amplified the apparent resident set size (we saw huge RSS spikes even after freeing many objects).

Evidence collected:
- Heap and RSS graphs from 10 representative pods attached to this incident (see linked confluence page).
- /internal/kvcache/stats showed resident_bytes increased 4–6x immediately after restart for affected pods.
- Trace of prefetch tasks: logs show repeated prefetch start entries for the same prefixes across ~10s windows with backoff resetting on every restart.
- Kernel OOMKill logs on nodes correspond to pods with the highest resident sizes.

Mitigation and recovery steps taken during incident:
- Disabled prefetch feature flag in prod: feature-flag/disable-prefetch = true (rollbackable).
- Manually forced an extra 30% capacity to the medium-gpu pool to reduce scheduling contention.
- Applied temporary run-time memory cap per pod (soft limit) to fail fast and avoid kernel OOMs while we stabilized capacity.
- Rolled a small patch to cancel in-flight prefetch tasks on SIGTERM (hotfix) and deployed to the pool within 22 minutes of detection (PR linked).

Why these mitigations worked:
- Disabling prefetch reduced simultaneous cache rebuild pressure on pods when restarted.
- Additional capacity reduced bin-packing pressure and prevented multiple large-resident pods from sharing the same host.
- Cancel-on-terminate prevented stale inflight tasks from continuing to allocate memory after termination began.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why did some pods exhibit RSS jumps even after the prefetch flag was disabled (allocator fragmentation?). Need heap dumps and jemalloc stats for affected releases.
- Is continuous-batching holding references across context cancellation in all code paths or only specific failure paths?
- Should cluster autoscaler be muted during provider maintenance windows or have hysteresis thresholds to avoid oscillatory replacement?

Permanent mitigations & follow-ups (action items):
- (A1) Implement global-rate-limit for prefetch across a pool so N concurrent prefetch tasks is bounded per pool. Owner: Marcus. Target: 3 weeks.
- (A2) Add robust cancelation to continuous-batching inflight handles and a safety timer to force release if shutdown stalls. Owner: Ravi. Target: 2 weeks.
- (A3) Work with runtime team to gather jemalloc/memory allocator metrics on next release; add jemalloc stats to metrics pipeline. Owner: Elena. Target: 4 weeks.
- (A4) Add autoscaler maintenance-mode flag that prevents aggressive scale decisions during known provider maintenance windows; integrate with provider webhooks. Owner: SRE Infra. Target: 6 weeks.
- (A5) Create a post-incident test in chaos lab that simulates mass pod restarts + prefetch enabled to validate safety limits. Owner: Oncall + Reliability Eng. Target: 4 weeks.
- (A6) Update serving runtime docs to recommend default prefetch throttles and expose them as config knobs. Owner: Product/Runtime. Target: 3 weeks.

Runbook updates (short):
- Add new play: "Prefetch storm during reschedule" under Serving Runtime incidents. Steps: 1) Check /internal/kvcache/stats for resident_bytes/alloc_counts, 2) Flip disable-prefetch flag, 3) Force scale up pool if >10% of pods are restarting concurrently, 4) If OOMs persist, set per-pod memory soft caps and apply cancellation patch.
- Add observability alert: add a composite alert that fires when (pod_restart_rate > 5% in 5m) AND (avg_prefetch_rate per pod > X).

Post-incident notes and follow-ups (brief):
- Hotfix PR (2781) implemented cancel-on-terminate for prefetch tasks; landed and rolled within incident window. Verify in staging before fully removing feature flag.
- We should prioritize jemalloc metrics because the RSS behavior is not fully explained by object counts alone.
- Customer comms: CS drafted an advisory; product agrees on a short blameless note to affected customers.

Appendix: useful commands & logs (on-call cheatsheet)
- Check pod memory: kubectl top pod -n redwood-serving | grep medium-gpu
- Check pod restarts: kubectl get pods -n redwood-serving -o wide --sort-by=.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount
- Check kvcache stats endpoint: curl -sS http://localhost:18000/internal/kvcache/stats | jq .resident_bytes
- Inspect node OOM logs: journalctl -k | grep -i oom
- Quick mitigations: curl -X POST "https://console.redwood.ai/api/flags/feature-flag/disable-prefetch" -H "Authorization: Bearer <ops-token>"

Notes to self (informal):
- Prefetch looked safe in normal operations but mass restarts uncovered terrible amplification. Need to treat warmup processes as first-class citizens for reschedule storms.
- Follow-up meeting scheduled 2024-10-18 with runtime/serving/infra/product to prioritize A1–A6.
- Next on-call: Marcus (week of 2024-10-21) — handoff doc linked in Slack.

Quotes from logs (raw snippets):
- "[03:12:14] prefetch: start prefixes N=214 last_restart=3s"
- "[03:12:38] kvcache: resident_bytes=61234567840 (growth +5.6x)"
- "[03:15:02] OOM killer invoked for pid 2314 (redwood-srv-007)"

Remaining artifacts to attach: heap dumps for pods srv-007 and srv-021 (request filed), jemalloc stats extraction task, follow-up GH issue to track autoscaler hysteresis (SRE-4123 child).

Status: in_review — feedback welcome on proposed priorities and runbook wording.

-- end of notes.
